name: Boehm-Demers-Weiser GC (bdwgc)
workload: Author's GC benchmark (small-object allocation heavy, C variant), modified to run multiple client threads sharing one heap; elapsed seconds for the GC build versus a malloc/free variant of the same benchmark.
claimed_speedup: docs/scale.md: thread-unsafe collector 9 s vs glibc malloc/free 10.51 s (pthreads not linked), about 1.17x (derived from page data); thread-safe collector (-D GC_THREADS) 10.3 s vs glibc malloc/free 20.90 s (one thread, pthreads linked), about 2.0x (derived from page data); two clients 23.5 s vs 24.55 s, about 1.04x (derived from page data). The same page states the benchmark favors a garbage collector since most objects are small. docs/overview.md claims, without numbers, that the collector may be faster for very small objects and slower for large ones, and may significantly outperform malloc/free with thread-local allocation.
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the baseline comparison (GC built with -D GC_THREADS; later table adds -D PARALLEL_MARK -D THREAD_LOCAL_ALLOC); optimization level unstated.
hardware: Dual-processor Pentium III/500, Linux 2.2.12, ancient GC release from 2000
stars_or_usage: 3.5k stars; packaged in many distributions (Repology badge in README)
tradeoffs: Conservative stack/heap scanning means false retention and no precise object layout; the docs say large-object allocation is slower than malloc and programs usually need more memory; collection pauses unless the incremental mode is used; thread-local allocation and parallel marking are build-time options; GC_MALLOC_ATOMIC and root hints are needed for best speed.
caveats: Only first-party numbers, from a roughly 25-year-old collector release on a Pentium III/500 under Linux 2.2.12 with an old glibc; compiler and flags unstated; the author says the workload favors a collector (mostly small objects). The benchmark source is hosted on the author's site (hboehm.info, not reachable from this session), so the run could not be reproduced from the repo. The single-thread figure is a modest 1.17x; the 2.0x figure compares a pthreads-linked malloc build, where glibc paid locking cost. The repo docs themselves say the collector is slower for large objects. A third-party 1992 technical report (Zorn, seen only as a search snippet) reports a trivial slowdown versus malloc/free but about twice the memory, so independent evidence points to competitive rather than faster. The license is the MIT-style permissive Boehm-GC text (SPDX Boehm-GC, not OSI-listed); a few GNU build files carry a modified GPL. The lead URL ivmai/bdwgc is the old home of this repository.

name: Cosmopolitan Libc (pthread_mutex_t)
workload: footek_test with USE POSIX: 30 threads each doing 100000 iterations of pthread_mutex_lock, increment a shared counter, pthread_mutex_unlock (heavily contended); wall time of the whole run on Linux 6.8.
claimed_speedup: Comment block in test/libc/thread/footek_test.c, 'with posix', Linux 6.8 AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX: cosmo 40,965 us real vs glibc 111,560 us real (about 2.7x faster, derived from page data) vs musl 392,765 us real (about 9.6x faster, derived from page data); user time 47,168 us (cosmo) vs 153,985 us (glibc) vs 1,885,558 us (musl). Other rows in the same file: FreeBSD cosmo 126,803 us vs freebsd libc 219,073 us; OpenBSD cosmo 138,619 us vs openbsd libc 385,431 us; Windows 10 cosmo 156,382 us vs Cygwin 9,334,610 us; but Apple M2 Ultra cosmo 65,118 us vs Apple libc 45,443 us (cosmo slower).
hardware: AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO 7995WX, Linux 6.8 (other rows: Apple M2 Ultra, FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, Windows 10 test machines)
tradeoffs: Cosmopolitan is a whole libc plus the Actually Portable Executable format, not a drop-in mutex library: using its mutex means building with cosmocc and linking its libc; some platform behavior differs from the host libc; the mutex code is tied to the libc's futex and thread internals.
caveats: Results are first-party comments pasted into a test file, one run each, no compiler or flags recorded, so tier C although the test source is public and the CPU is named. Only a single highly contended 30-thread microbenchmark; it says nothing about uncontended lock cost or other libc facilities. On Apple M2 Ultra the same file shows Cosmo slower than Apple's libc. The maintainer's blog post on mutexes (justine.lol, not reachable from this session) is reported by search snippets with slightly different figures (36,905 us vs 101,353 us for glibc, and 2.75x over Windows SRWLOCK); those were not opened and are not used. The lead describes the project only as 'fast portable static native textmode containers'; the project's other speed claims (startup 400 us faster with binfmt_misc registration, README) have no baseline numbers.

name: cpp-lazy
baseline: std::ranges / std::views (libstdc++ 13): filter, chunk, chunk_by, lazy_split, stride, slide, zip, cartesian_product, repeat, take, join
workload: Google Benchmark microbenchmarks over 32-element arrays and a 32-character string: one pass over each lazy iterable with benchmark::DoNotOptimize on each element (iterable creation excluded), lz:: adaptor versus the matching std::views adaptor, built as C++23.
claimed_speedup: README Benchmarks section plus bench/benchmarks-iterators-23.png, per-iteration column (lz vs std): filter 0.2263 ns vs 0.8116 ns (about 3.6x faster, derived from page data); chunks 0.2425 ns vs 0.6376 ns (about 2.6x); split_multiple (lz::split vs views::lazy_split on a string) 0.4866 ns vs 0.8532 ns (about 1.75x); split_single 0.3902 ns vs 0.5568 ns (about 1.4x); chunk_if 0.4922 ns vs 0.5351 ns (about 1.09x); flatten 0.7095 ns vs 0.7771 ns (about 1.10x). Parity within about 1 to 4 percent: map 0.2384 vs 0.2374, repeat 0.2389 vs 0.2372, take_iterable 0.2397 vs 0.2378, take_iterator 0.2389 vs 0.2386, common 0.2399 vs 0.2386, pairwise 0.4477 vs 0.4602, zip2/zip3/zip4 0.4904/0.7233/0.9545 vs 0.4764/0.7238/0.9582, cartesian_product 1.1439 vs 1.1684. Slower than std: take_every 0.9186 ns vs 0.5455 ns for std::views::stride (about 1.7x slower).
compiler_and_flags: gcc 13.3.0 (README); optimization flags and C++ standard not stated in README, bench is built as C++23 (file name suffix 23, std::views::chunk and stride need it)
tradeoffs: Works in C++11 through C++23 (the std views need C++20/23), so it fills the gap for older standards; lz iterables hold references to non-view inputs (maybe_owned) unless copied; sentinel-based ranges need workarounds before C++17; API differs from std::ranges (lz::filter(...), not views::filter) and the library is far smaller than range-v3.
caveats: First-party benchmark with public code but no CPU model, no optimization flags and the standard library only implied (libstdc++ inferred from gcc 13.3.0), so tier C. Tiny workload: 32 elements, the filter predicate matches only the first element, so the 3.6x filter figure measures a scan for the first match, where std::views::filter also caches begin(); most other rows are at parity, and std::views::stride beats lz::take_every by 1.7x. The benchmark image labels columns 'lz (1 iteration / 32 iterations)'; the first number equals the second divided by 32. Results come from a single PNG with no run-to-run variance and no comparison against range-v3. The repo was formerly MarcDirven/cpp-lazy (the lead URL) and now lives at Kaaserne/cpp-lazy. The lead's suggested category (filesystems-and-io) does not fit; this is a ranges/iterator library, so it is filed under stdlib-replacements with a new category name for the orchestrator to remap.
